summary.text: A chemical reaction turns one set of chemical substances into another by rearranging atoms, and it comes with an energy change.
The starting substances are called reactants, and the products they yield usually have properties different from them.
Some reactions produce heat, others may require heat, and reaction rates typically increase as temperature rises.

paragraphs.heading: Substances into new substances
paragraphs.text: A chemical reaction turns one set of substances into a different set. As it happens, the atoms are rearranged into new products, and there is a change in energy. The starting substances are called reactants, or reagents. What comes out are the products, which usually have different properties from what went in.

paragraphs.heading: Only the electrons move
paragraphs.text: In the classic sense, a reaction changes only where electrons sit as bonds between atoms break and form. The nuclei are left alone, so the elements present stay the same. Nuclear chemistry is different: it deals with unstable, radioactive elements, where the nuclei can change too. The idea of a reaction has also been stretched to cover things smaller than atoms, such as radioactive decay and reactions between elementary particles.

paragraphs.heading: Writing reactions down
paragraphs.text: Chemists describe reactions with chemical equations. Reactants go on the left, products on the right, and an arrow between them, read as "yields", points the way the reaction runs. A double arrow, ⇌, marks an equilibrium reaction. An equation must be balanced, so each kind of atom appears the same number of times on both sides.

paragraphs.heading: Heat and speed
paragraphs.text: Each reaction runs at a characteristic rate for a given temperature and concentration. Exothermic reactions give off heat, while endothermic reactions need heat put in before they can happen. Warming things up usually speeds a reaction, because more thermal energy is on hand to reach the activation energy needed to break bonds. Many reactions are really a chain of smaller steps called elementary reactions, and the detailed route they take is the reaction mechanism.

paragraphs.heading: Reactions in living things
paragraphs.text: In living things, reactions link into chains called metabolic pathways, where the product of one step becomes the reactant of the next. Protein enzymes often speed these steps up. That lets a cell build and break down molecules, work that would be impossible under ordinary conditions, at the temperature and concentrations found inside it.

paragraphs.heading: From alchemy to industry
paragraphs.text: People have used reactions such as burning, fermentation and turning ores into metals since ancient times. Medieval alchemists studied chemical change, trying in particular to turn lead into gold. In the 17th century Johann Rudolph Glauber made hydrochloric acid by reacting sulfuric acid with sodium chloride. Reactions moved into industry with the lead chamber process of 1746 and the Leblanc process, followed in the 1880s by the contact process, and in 1909–1910 by the Haber process for making ammonia.

paragraphs.heading: Getting the ideas right
paragraphs.text: Explaining reactions took time. In 1667 Johann Joachim Becher proposed that things that burn contain a fire-like element, phlogiston, which escapes when they burn. Antoine Lavoisier showed in 1785 that this was false: burning is a reaction with oxygen from the air. Chemists also long believed that substances from living things carried a special vital force and could not be made in the lab. Friedrich Wöhler ended that split in 1828 by making urea from inorganic starting materials.
